implementation_notes: Unity owns the loop and exposes the pattern's two phases as callbacks: FixedUpdate is 'Update called at regular, fixed intervals as part of Unity's physics update loop', with the interval set by Time.fixedDeltaTime (default 0.02 s, 50 calls per second), and it 'may be called zero, one, or multiple times per frame depending on the frame rate and simulation needs'; Update is called once per rendered frame. What replaces the classic structure: the engine's player loop replaces the driver and the accumulator - FixedUpdate is the fixed-step update, Update the variable render tick - and the roles collapse into MonoBehaviour callbacks, with input read in Update and physics integrated by the engine between FixedUpdate calls. Use Time.deltaTime for presentation logic and Time.fixedDeltaTime for per-step coefficients, and let Rigidbody interpolation provide the smoothness a hand-written alpha would.
pitfalls: FixedUpdate can run zero or several times per rendered frame, so input sampling, camera smoothing and UI work placed there behaves unevenly - keep it to simulation and leave presentation to Update/LateUpdate.
Time.deltaTime is the render step, not the physics step: using it to advance forces or accumulators double-applies time once FixedUpdate runs several times per frame.
Changing Time.fixedDeltaTime at runtime alters physics fidelity and cost, and tuned constants assume the old step; treat it as a build-time decision, and remember Time.timeScale scales both clocks.
Physics contacts, raycasts and velocity changes made in Update are applied at the next fixed step, so mixing the phases yields one-step-late input and jitter.

variants.name: MonoGame Game loop with a fixed time step
variants.implementation_notes: MonoGame's Game 'runs a game loop that calls Update(GameTime) and Draw(GameTime)'; with IsFixedTimeStep 'the target time between frames is given by TargetElapsedTime', and MaxElapsedTime bounds 'the maximum amount of time we will frameskip over and only perform Update calls with no Draw calls'. What replaces the classic structure: the framework implements the pattern's fixed-update/variable-render split - Update runs on the TargetElapsedTime cadence, Draw runs as often as the platform allows, and the frame-skip cap is a built-in spiral-of-death guard. Under fixed step gameTime.ElapsedGameTime equals TargetElapsedTime, so Update can use it directly as dt; Draw must render the current state and never advance the simulation.
variants.idiom_name: Game.IsFixedTimeStep with TargetElapsedTime, Update(GameTime) and Draw(GameTime)
pitfalls: Under fixed step ElapsedGameTime repeats TargetElapsedTime, so using the delta is safe only inside Update; Draw must not advance the simulation.
Setting IsFixedTimeStep = false hands real, variable frame times to Update - the classic unstable configuration; keeping it false means owning the clamp and a bounded step yourself.
MaxElapsedTime (the frameskip cap) is what prevents runaway catch-up; removing it or making it huge re-enables the spiral of death.

variants.name: Hand-written Stopwatch loop (no engine)
variants.implementation_notes: Without an engine, .NET supplies only the measurement half: Stopwatch 'provides a set of methods and properties that you can use to accurately measure elapsed time', with Stopwatch.IsHighResolution and Stopwatch.Frequency exposing the underlying timer and Elapsed returning a TimeSpan. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - write the driver loop over Stopwatch.GetTimestamp()/Elapsed and pace with Thread.Sleep or a timer. This is the right shape for headless servers, tools, simulation tests and console harnesses, where there is no player loop, and it keeps the simulation step decoupled from any UI. Message-loop hosts (WPF, WinForms, MAUI) should instead use their dispatcher timer facilities so the UI thread stays responsive.
pitfalls: Thread.Sleep(1) sleeps for at least a millisecond and typically longer (timer granularity); derive cadence from Stopwatch elapsed values, not from loop counts.
Stopwatch.Elapsed allocates and consults the high-resolution counter; in an allocation-sensitive loop read GetTimestamp() and divide by Stopwatch.Frequency instead.

A busy loop with no Sleep pins a core and defeats the power argument for a paced loop; conversely, sleeping on the UI thread freezes the application - run the loop on its own thread or use a dispatcher timer.
